hero.deck: The rollout phase is over, and the project plan that used to live here has done its job. What's left is simpler, and it comes down to three things: use the tool you're actually comfortable in, build and maintain the knowledge base that makes any of them useful, and do all of it out in the open where we can learn from each other. First, though, one practical thing: if something's broken, there's now a five-second way to tell me. Everything after that is reference — the terms, how the technology works, how we handle data.

bugTracker.title: IF SOMETHING'S BROKEN, TELL ME.
bugTracker.deck: Some of what's been set up doesn't work right yet. That isn't a failure — it's what the first few rounds of any deployment look like. What doesn't help is somebody quietly working around a broken tool for three weeks.
bugTracker.introHtml:
I've heard from a few of you that some of the Claude Teams tools are broken or aren't behaving the way they should. That's fair, and it's accurate. I've been installing all of this about as fast as I can, and with something this complicated it normally takes a few iterations to get right.

So if a connector returns nothing, a skill misfires, or a tool just doesn't do what it claims to — that's useful information. I'd far rather hear it than have you assume it's meant to work that way. There's now a proper way to report it, and it takes about five seconds.

steps.title: Say what's wrong
steps.body: In the AI channel in Google Chat, type the issue in plain language. “The Shopify connector returns nothing for wholesale orders” is plenty — you don't need to diagnose it.

steps.title: Add a screenshot if it helps
steps.body: Optional. If the problem is visual, or the error message is long and fiddly to retype, a screenshot saves a round trip.

steps.title: Hit enter. You're done.
steps.body: That's the entire report. No form, no ticket number to keep track of, nothing else expected from you.

then: It sends me an email alert straight away.
It's logged in the bug tracker — a project plan in Google Sheets — and assigned as a task, so it can't get buried in the scroll.
I pick it up, or hand it to an agent to work on. Sometimes it's a real bug and gets fixed; sometimes it's a five-minute answer, or simply a better way to do the thing.
bugTracker.noteHtml: This is how tech teams at bigger companies handle it — everything routes through a tracker so problems stay visible and countable instead of living in DMs and getting forgotten. Given how complicated AI tooling is right now, it makes sense for us too.

requiredReading.title: Read me first — getting set up (Claude)
requiredReading.summary: A 10-minute orientation for anyone on Claude. On ChatGPT, Gemini or Grok instead? The concepts carry over — ask Jonathan for the equivalent setup.
requiredReading.body_md:
## Welcome to Claude Teams at Pappy & Co

You've just been added to our Claude Teams workspace. This is your **first stop** — a 10-minute orientation before you start building, drafting, analyzing, or asking.

> **A note on platforms.** Claude is one of the options, not the only one. If you've chosen ChatGPT, Gemini or Grok for your company seat, the concepts in this guide — the different surfaces, private vs. shared work, and especially the data-handling tiers — carry over almost exactly; ask Jonathan for the equivalent setup. **The data rules below apply on every platform, without exception.**

> 📄 **The full Welcome Kit (with diagrams, all customizers, and example asks) is here:** [Open the Pappy & Co Claude Welcome Kit (PDF)](./brands/pappy-co/assets/welcome-kit.pdf)

The summary below covers the critical bits. Open the PDF for the complete version.

---

## Step 00 — before anything else

### Download the Claude Mac app. Don't start in Chrome.

The single most important thing you'll do this week. Go to **[claude.ai/download](https://claude.ai/download)**, install the macOS desktop app, and sign in with your Pappy & Co email. **Use the desktop app as your daily driver** — not the browser tab.

**Why this matters:** The browser version is sandboxed. It can't read or write files on your Mac, can't open your selected folder, can't run scripts, and has limited connector behavior. If you start in Chrome you'll think Claude is less capable than it actually is — and you'll waste a week wondering why everyone else's Claude can build XLSX files and yours can't. *Install the app first. Everything below assumes you have.*

---

## The three doors — Cowork, Chat, Code

Same Claude underneath. Different surface. Each one is built for a different shape of work — and the wrong door makes the job slower, not faster.

### 1 · Cowork (desktop app · files & connectors)
**For getting actual work shipped.** Cowork is a desktop app that gives Claude a workspace folder on your Mac plus a sandboxed Linux shell. It can read your selected folder, write new files, run scripts, build spreadsheets and decks, and call our connected tools.

*Good for: build a wholesale deck, pull last month's Shopify orders into XLSX, reorganize supplier PDFs, draft + send a Klaviyo campaign brief.*

### 2 · Chat (web · mobile · quick thinking)
**For thinking, drafting, and asking.** The classic Claude surface — claude.ai in your browser or the mobile app. No file system. Great for drafts, conversations, brainstorms, and questions that don't need to touch our systems.

*Good for: draft a Slack message, brainstorm Q3 cigar subscription messaging, summarize a vendor PDF you paste in, quick GA4 question.*

### 3 · Code (terminal · repos · for developers)
**For when the work lives in a repo.** Claude Code is a CLI that runs in your terminal and operates inside a git repository. Edits code, runs tests, opens PRs. If you don't write code day-to-day, you don't need this — Cowork covers nearly every operator workflow.

### Rule of thumb
> If the answer should land as a **file** on your computer, open Cowork.
> If you want a **conversation**, stay in Chat.
> If you're touching a **repo**, you're in Code.

---

## What's wired up for you

The full PDF lists every connector and skill in detail. The headline list:

**Operations & commerce:** Shopify (retail + wholesale), Cin7 Core, Inventory Planner, Klaviyo, Attentive, Gorgias, GA4, Google Workspace, Notion + Asana.

**Working & communication:** Slack, Zoom, DocuSign, LinkedIn, Canva, Apollo + Common Room.

**Pappy-specific skills:** Brand Kit (always-on — triggers when you ask for branded output), Brand Voice Enforcement (on-demand reviewer), Productivity (persistent memory of our team + projects + shorthand).

**Skill packs we lean on:** marketing, sales, customer support, finance, HR, ops, legal, data, design, engineering, PM — invoke with a slash command (e.g. `/marketing:campaign-plan`) or just describe what you need.

You don't have to install any of this. It's available the moment your invite goes through.

---

## Privacy — private chats vs. shared projects

The most-asked question on day one: *"Can the team see what I just typed?"* **Short answer: only if you put it in a Project that's set to share with the workspace.**

🔒 **Private (default).** When you open a new chat from the Claude home screen, it lives in your account only. No one in the workspace can read it — not Jonathan, not admins. One-off questions, brainstorms, drafts → keep them private. Sensitive HR or 1:1 conversations → private.

🔗 **Shared via Projects.** When you create a Project and set it to "Share with workspace," every chat inside that project is visible to other teammates with access. Files, custom instructions, and chats become team-readable. Use this for cross-functional work, shared SOPs, ongoing initiatives.

> **Practical rule:** If two or more people will benefit from continuity on a topic, make it a shared Project. If it's "just me thinking out loud," keep it in a private chat. When in doubt — start private. You can always move work into a shared Project later.

Anthropic doesn't train on Pappy's data. Default-deny is enforced at the workspace level.

---

## Our data handling tiers — non-negotiable

You will run into sensitive data. Our policy classifies it into four tiers — **treat the tier as the ceiling**. Don't move data to a less-restricted tier without checking with Jonathan first.

| Tier | What it is | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **1 · NEVER** | Secrets | API keys, passwords, OAuth tokens, signing secrets, payment processor credentials, 2FA recovery codes. **Never paste these into any AI tool, ever.** |
| **2 · DON'T** | Regulated PII | Customer credit card numbers, CVVs, bank info, SSNs, government IDs, login credentials, age-verification docs. |
| **3 · APPROVED TOOLS ONLY** | Confidential business data | Wholesale pricing, supplier costs (Cin7), contracts, P&L, payroll, headcount, unreleased product info, customer lists. Company-provided seats only — never personal AI accounts. |
| **4 · GENERALLY FINE** | Internal but low-risk | Aggregated analytics, public marketing copy, published product info, GA4 reports without PII, draft creative, general SOPs. |

**Hard rules:** Never connect a personal AI account to company data. Never share logins. Never use customer data for AI training. Never paste a Tier 1 secret anywhere. *If in doubt, ask Jonathan before pasting, uploading, or connecting.*

---

## Your first 30 minutes — quick start

Run through this once and you're operational. Most of it is pre-wired — you're really just signing in and trying things.

1. **Most important — download the Mac app** from [claude.ai/download](https://claude.ai/download). Not Chrome.
2. **Accept your Claude Teams invite** and sign into the Mac app. You'll land in the Pappy & Co workspace automatically.
3. **Open Cowork mode** in the Mac app, select a working folder (Desktop or a project folder is fine), and try a small ask.
4. **In your first chat, ask:** *"What customizers and connectors do I have access to?"* — Claude will list them.
5. **Try a real task** from the examples in the PDF. The brand kit will trigger automatically when relevant.
6. **Decide private vs. shared.** Is this work better as a private chat or a shared Project? Make a Project for anything ongoing.
7. **Re-read the data tiers above.** Bookmark them. Send Jonathan questions, not pastes.
8. **Send Jonathan one workflow** you'd love to automate this quarter. We'll wire it up.

---

> 📄 **Read the full Welcome Kit PDF for the complete version** — example asks for every team, the rest of the connectors and skill packs, the full design treatment.
> **[→ Open the Welcome Kit PDF](./brands/pappy-co/assets/welcome-kit.pdf)**

---

## Questions?

Ask in the AI channel in Google Chat — that's the point of it — or email Jonathan directly.

*Welcome Kit v1.0 · April 2026 · Maintained by Jonathan Nichols*

requiredReading.title: The ground rules for using AI here
requiredReading.summary: What's fine to do, what's not, and how oversight works — on whichever AI platform you've chosen.
requiredReading.body_md:
## The short version
Everyone gets a company AI seat. Which platform that seat is on is up to you — Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok. Here's how to use it well, whichever one you picked.

## You can
- Draft emails, Gorgias replies, reports, product copy, briefs, wholesale outreach — and use them within whatever workflow your team has agreed for that kind of work
- Ask it questions about how Pappy does things — it can look up our SOPs, brand standards, marketing playbooks and vendor history ("The Vault")
- Use it with the connected tools (Shopify, Cin7, Klaviyo, Attentive, Gorgias, GA4) to pull current info

## Please don't
- Paste sensitive stuff into it — full customer lists, payment details, anyone's personal records, confidential wholesale account terms
- Use a personal or free AI account for Pappy work — use the company seat you've been given, signed in with your @pappyco.com account. The platform is your choice; using a personal account is not
- Change how automated a workflow is on your own — that's a team decision, not a solo one

## How much oversight?
**Your team decides, workflow by workflow.** Some work gets a person reviewing everything; some runs more automated once everyone's confident; it changes over time. The Pappy brand kit and voice profiles are the source of truth for how things sound and look — not the model's defaults. When you're not sure where a workflow falls, ask Jonathan — and when in doubt, more oversight, not less.

## Questions?
Ask your manager, or Jonathan — or just ask in the AI channel in Google Chat, where everyone benefits from the answer.

requiredReading.title: What happens to our data
requiredReading.summary: Plain answers: where data goes, what stays out of the AI entirely, and how the Tier 1–4 sorting works.
requiredReading.body_md:
## The plain version
People worry about this, fairly. Here's where things stand.

## We sort information by how sensitive it is
- **Tier 1 — never goes near the AI.** Full customer lists, payment data, employee records.
- **Tier 2 — connected tools only, never pasted into chat.** Revenue figures, wholesale account terms, supplier pricing.
- **Tier 3 — lives in "The Vault."** SOPs, marketing playbooks, campaign history, brand standards.
- **Tier 4 — share-with-the-team.** Roadmaps, training guides, this portal.

## These tiers apply on every platform
Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok — it makes no difference. The tiers are about where Pappy's information is allowed to go, not about which vendor you picked.

## How the connections work
The links to Shopify, Cin7, Klaviyo, Attentive, Gorgias and GA4 are scoped down to only what a task actually needs, and read-only wherever possible. A connector that returns more than a task needs is a bug — we report it, we don't work around it.

## This page
This page carries Tier 4 only. If Tier 3 data ever needed to live here, we'd add a stronger access gate first.

## If you ever spot something that doesn't sit right
Say so — to your manager or Jonathan. Take it seriously; we will too.

requiredReading.title: How we use Google Drive with AI (and why it works)
requiredReading.summary: Google Drive holds the truth. The AI reads from it. This is the thinking behind the knowledge base.
requiredReading.body_md: > **This doc says "Claude" throughout because that's what we started on. It applies identically to ChatGPT, Gemini or Grok — the argument is about Drive being the source of truth, not about which AI reads it.** ## The short version **Google Drive is where our documents live. The AI is what reads them, on demand, in the context of a question.** Drive handles storage and version control like it always has — we don't change how the team writes, edits, or shares files. Claude becomes the smart reader on top: ask it about an SOP, and it pulls the current version from Drive, reads it, and answers in plain language using what's actually written down. You don't move documents into Claude. You don't copy-paste from Drive into a chat. You point Claude at the Drive file, and Claude reads it when needed. ## Why Google Drive stays in charge Drive is the **source of truth**. That means: - **One copy.** Everyone's looking at the same document, not a fork inside an AI tool. - **Version history.** Drive remembers every change anyone has ever made. If the brand voice doc gets a bad edit, we can roll it back in two clicks. - **Permissions you already understand.** Sharing rules are Google's — who can view, comment, edit. We don't reinvent it. - **Edit anywhere.** Phone, laptop, Docs, Word, third-party tools. Drive doesn't care; the document keeps working. - **Search you already know.** ⌘+K in Drive finds things by filename and full text the way it always has. If we instead uploaded documents *into* Claude as fixed copies, the moment someone updates the original in Drive, Claude would be reading a stale version. The mismatch becomes invisible — Claude sounds confident, but it's quoting a doc that no longer exists. That's the failure mode we're avoiding. ## Why Claude is the smart reader, not the storage Claude's job is **inference** — turning a question into an answer that uses the documents it can see. It's great at: - Reading several long documents at once and writing a coherent summary - Pulling the relevant paragraph out of a 40-page SOP - Catching what a doc doesn't say ("the policy doesn't mention returns") - Writing in the same voice as the source material What Claude is bad at: - Being trusted as a vault. Don't make Claude the only place a document exists. - Remembering the last conversation forever. Each chat is fresh; what carries over is the project's files and instructions, not the chat history. - Quoting fixed numbers from memory. It might *paraphrase* a number wrong. Always have it cite the source. So the architecture is: > **Drive = persistent memory.** > **Claude = the part that thinks.** They each do what they're best at. ## How to actually do it 1. **Document lives in Drive** like always. Edit it where you'd normally edit it. 2. **Attach the Drive link to your Claude project** (Claude Teams projects have a "Files" panel — paste the Drive URL or upload). For a one-off question, you can also paste the link inside the chat. 3. **Ask Claude about it.** "Read the wholesale onboarding SOP I just added, and draft a follow-up email for an account that hasn't replied in two weeks." 4. **When the Drive doc changes**, Claude picks up the new version next time it reads. You don't have to re-upload — the reference is to the live file. 5. **Cite your source.** Ask Claude to quote the section it used. If the answer is fuzzy, that usually means the source doc itself is fuzzy — fix it in Drive, and the answer improves everywhere. ## Why this combination works It's a **separation of concerns**, which is just engineer-speak for "two things, each doing what it's best at": | Drive does | Claude does | |---|---| | Stores the file forever | Reads it when asked | | Tracks every version | Reasons about the current one | | Handles permissions | Stays within whatever Drive allows it to see | | Lets people edit collaboratively | Doesn't try to be a document editor | | Search by filename and exact text | Search by meaning — finds the relevant section even if the words don't match | The combination gives us: - **No duplication.** One document, one place. The thing on Drive is the thing. - **Privacy by default.** Drive holds the data. Claude reads only what we let it see, when we ask. It doesn't keep a permanent copy. - **Updates are free.** No "sync the AI" step. Edit in Drive, Claude reads the new version next time. - **Version control is built in.** When we change how we do something, the change history is in Drive, not buried in Claude chat logs. - **Hybrid search.** Drive's keyword search + Claude's meaning-based search. Use both — they find different things. ## Common gotchas - **Permission mismatches.** Claude can only read what your account has access to in Drive. If a doc is "only me," Claude can't see it in a shared project. Open access in Drive first. - **Stale screenshots.** If you take a screenshot of a Google Doc and paste the image into Claude, you've broken the live link. Just paste the URL. - **Whole-folder references.** Claude can read a Drive folder, but the more files in the folder, the slower and fuzzier the answer. Point it at the specific docs that matter. - **Don't ask Claude to "save" something to Drive yet.** That's a workflow we'd build separately. For now: Claude drafts, you save to Drive. ## What about The Vault? The Vault (the RAG library) is the **always-on** version of this same idea — a curated subset of documents that every project automatically has access to, indexed so even very large libraries are fast to search. Project-level Drive references are the **on-demand, project-specific** version. Use Drive references when: - The doc is specific to one project or one person's work - The doc changes often and you want the latest version each time - The doc is too operational to belong in the core The Vault library Use The Vault when: - It's a foundational SOP, brand standard, or playbook every project should know about - You want it indexed for fast semantic search across hundreds of docs The two work well together — The Vault is the company's memory, Drive references are the working drafts. ## Questions? Ask your manager, or Jonathan — or raise it in the AI channel in Google Chat.

requiredReading.title: How to actually use the workspace
requiredReading.summary: Day-one orientation: your private space vs. the team space, where shared instructions and the brand kit live, and what to do when you're stuck.
requiredReading.body_md:
## Your space vs. the team's space
Every company AI platform works this way — Claude Teams, ChatGPT Business, and the rest. There are two kinds of areas:
- **Your own private space** — only you see it. Use it for drafts, half-formed ideas, scratch work, anything not ready to share.
- **The shared team space** — this holds the approved reusable instructions, the brand kit and the project know-how everyone draws from. Changes here affect the whole team, so treat it like the shared drive: don't reorganize it on a whim.

A simple rule: **if you wouldn't put it in the company Google Drive, keep it in your private space.**

## The shared instructions ("skills")
For common tasks — wholesale bundles, Cerity reports, Gorgias macros, Klaviyo flows, product copy — there are pre-written instructions you can call up by name, so you don't start from a blank box every time. If one needs changing, tell whoever owns it (see Team & Ownership) rather than editing it yourself.

## Cost
The workspace is paid for centrally. There's no per-person charge — use it for Pappy work as much as you like.

## When you're stuck
Ask in the AI channel in Google Chat. Answering it there means the next person doesn't have to ask twice — that's the whole idea.

yourData.title: WHAT WE WILL — AND WON'T — DO WITH IT.
yourData.deck: Being straight about this matters more than anything else on the page. Here it is, both sides.
will: Connect the AI to your work tools (Shopify, Cin7, Klaviyo, Attentive, Gorgias, GA4, Workspace) — scoped to the minimum a task needs, read-only wherever we can
Load Pappy's own know-how — SOPs, playbooks, vendor history, brand standards, product specs — into "The Vault" for the AI to answer from
Curate the knowledge base — approving what goes in, retiring what's gone stale, and resolving documents that contradict each other, so answers come from current material
Keep this page to the Tier-4 (share-with-the-team) kind of information only
Tell you, plainly, anytime that changes
wont: Put full customer lists, payment details, employee records or confidential wholesale terms anywhere near the AI or this page
Turn on automation for a workflow without the team agreeing the level of oversight first
Use Pappy's data to train some outside company's AI model
Connect a tool with broader access than the work actually requires
yourData.note: If anything here ever stops being true, you'll hear it from us first — not discover it later. And if a connection or a setting ever looks off to you, flag it; "reconnect it with more access to make it work" is never the answer.

underTheHood.title: The technical version — for whoever wants it
underTheHood.hint: Click to expand. None of this is required reading — it's here for the curious, and for anyone who likes to know exactly what's being plugged in.
underTheHood.deck: The same three areas, described the way an AI person would describe them. None of this is required reading — it's here for the curious, and for anyone who likes to know exactly what's plugged into what.

blocks.title: The model layer — your choice of platform
blocks.bodyHtml: Company seats on Claude Teams (Anthropic), ChatGPT Business (OpenAI), or Gemini / Grok — one seat per person, chosen by the person. All are frontier-class and broadly interchangeable for our work. What's enforced is the plan tier, not the vendor: company plans mean no training on our data, admin control, and SSO. The differentiator we actually invest in is the knowledge layer below, which is deliberately vendor-neutral.

blocks.title: The knowledge base — retrieval layer
blocks.bodyHtml: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) layer indexed over our own material: SOPs, processes, tribal knowledge, vendor and financial contracts, brand standards, campaign history. Chunked and tagged with structured metadata (type, vendor, effective date, owner) so retrieval is precise rather than fuzzy. Built on open formats and portable across platforms by design — the ingest path is a Google Chat submission, with weekly human approval before anything is indexed.

blocks.title: MCP connectors — the data layer
blocks.bodyHtml: The "connections to your tools" are MCP servers (Model Context Protocol) for Shopify Plus (retail + wholesale), Cin7 Core, Klaviyo, Attentive, Gorgias, GA4 and Google Workspace. Live data, model-agnostic, least privilege and read-only wherever possible. Credentials in a secret store, never in a prompt or a repo.

blocks.title: Creative & imaging stack
blocks.bodyHtml: Adobe Photoshop + Illustrator + Firefly (3 seats), with Firefly bridged to Drive and Shopify via Zapier, plus Claude Design for concepting. Firefly is rights-clear and brand-tunable; Claude can't generate native images and doesn't need to.

blocks.title: Voice profiles + skills
blocks.bodyHtml: Pappy's voice as per-channel tone profiles (retail email, wholesale, customer service, internal ops), plus a prompt and skills library authored as markdown — portable plain text rather than a proprietary format, so it moves between platforms as people switch.

blocks.title: Evals — the quality layer
blocks.bodyHtml: An evaluation harness runs on the critical workflows — customer-service response quality, copy on-brand-ness, wholesale reply rates — so "is it good?" is something we measure, not something we guess.

glossarySection.title: WHAT WE MEAN WHEN WE SAY…
glossarySection.deck: If a word in here ever made you go "huh?", it's probably below. Nobody's expected to know these going in.

glossary.plainHtml: Software that's very good at working with text — drafting, summarizing, answering questions, pulling things together. It's a strong drafter and a fast researcher; it is not a source of truth, which is why a person checks its work.
One of the AI platforms available here, made by a company called Anthropic. "Claude Teams" is the shared, secure company version — the same idea as a company ChatGPT plan, just a different vendor.
A feature inside Claude for visual concepting — sketching layouts and packaging ideas — separate from the production work that happens in Photoshop, Illustrator and Firefly.
What you type to the AI — your question or instruction. Better, more specific prompts get better answers, same as a clearer brief to a coworker.

"RAG" stands for "retrieval-augmented generation." Plainly: this is the knowledge base — a library of our documents (SOPs, playbooks, vendor history, contracts, brand standards) that the AI looks things up in before it answers, so it replies from how Pappy does things rather than the open internet. We've called it "The Vault"; it's the same thing.
A standard way to plug the AI into a tool you already use (Shopify, Cin7, Klaviyo, Gorgias) so it can see current information instead of a stale export. "MCP" is just the name of the standard.
Adobe's AI image tool — generates and edits images that are commercially safe to use and can be tuned to Pappy's look. It's how we'll do AI imagery, not ChatGPT.

An AI set up to handle a particular job mostly on its own — like "draft the wholesale follow-up emails" — within rules a person set. Increasingly this is what people mean by using AI well: you hand off a task and it works while you do something else.

A pre-written set of instructions for a common task — wholesale bundles, Cerity reports, Gorgias macros — saved so you can call it up by name instead of starting from scratch. Stored as plain text so it's easy to read, change and keep.
Logging into the AI workspace with your existing @pappyco.com account, instead of yet another username and password.
A quality check — a repeatable test that scores how good the AI's output is on the tasks that matter (is the Gorgias reply helpful? is the copy on-brand?). So quality is measured, not assumed.
Our way of sorting information by how sensitive it is — from "share with the team" (Tier 4, this page) up to "never goes near the AI" (Tier 1: full customer lists, payment data, personnel records).
The company that makes Claude. Founded by ex-OpenAI researchers; their thing is safety-focused AI. They're the vendor behind our Claude Teams subscription.

Different AI company, different assistant — and one of the platforms you can pick here. ChatGPT is what most people have tried at home. If it's the tool you're comfortable in, use it: ask Jonathan for a company seat and the desktop setup. What matters isn't the brand — it's that you're on a company seat rather than a personal free account, so Pappy's information stays inside Pappy.

Google's AI, built into Google Workspace (Gmail, Docs, Drive). You'll see it pop up in the corner of your Google apps. It's a legitimate choice for your seat too — one seat per person, whichever platform you prefer. Same rule as everywhere else: a company seat, not a personal account.

Microsoft's AI assistant (and GitHub's coding assistant — same name, different products). You'll hear it a lot in the business press. Not one of the platforms we've set up, but useful to know what people mean.

The three sizes of Claude. Opus is the biggest/smartest (and slowest/most expensive). Sonnet is the balanced one most work runs on. Haiku is fast and cheap, for simple tasks. You usually don't have to pick — Claude Teams uses the right one for the job.

How AI counts text. Roughly 4 characters or ¾ of a word. Pricing and the size of what fits in one conversation are measured in tokens. You don't have to count them — just know that very long prompts or huge documents can hit limits.

How much text Claude can "see at once" in a conversation — everything you've said, everything it's said, every file you've attached. Modern Claude can hold roughly a 200-page book in context. When a conversation gets very long, it starts to forget the early bits — start a fresh chat if that happens.

When the AI makes something up that sounds confident but isn't true. The classic one is inventing a citation or a customer name. This is why a person checks its work — especially on numbers, dates, names, and anything quoted as fact. The Vault helps a lot here because it pulls from real Pappy documents instead of guessing.

A dial for how creative vs. predictable the AI's answer is. Low = same answer every time (good for structured stuff). High = more variation (good for brainstorming taglines). You won't usually touch this — skills set it for you.

The text an AI model was taught on — a big chunk of the public internet plus licensed books and code. Importantly: your conversations on a company seat are not used to train future models. That's a key reason we use company plans rather than consumer ones, on every platform.

Taking a general AI model and giving it extra training on a specific company's stuff so it sounds more like them. We mostly don't do this — The Vault (RAG) gets us 95% of the way there without the cost or complexity.

Invisible instructions Claude gets at the start of every conversation in a project ("You're a wholesale-team assistant for Pappy & Co; sound like X; always use The Vault for facts; etc."). You don't write this — it's set up per project.

A workspace inside Claude Teams for one kind of work — "Wholesale outreach," "Gorgias replies," "Brand voice." A project carries its own files, instructions, and chat history, so you're not setting context from scratch every time.
Documents you attach to a project so Claude can read them — SOPs, brand kit, customer scripts. Different from The Vault (which is bigger and indexed): files are the local, project-specific stuff.
Claude's saved output — a code block, a long doc, a chart — shown in a side panel you can preview and copy. "Open the artifact" just means "look at the thing Claude built in the side panel."
Persistent notes you give Claude about yourself or how you want answers ("I work in wholesale; be concise; always use Pappy voice"). Set once, apply to every chat in that project.

Application Programming Interface — the way one piece of software talks to another, with no human in the middle. When we say "connect Shopify via API," we mean software-to-software, automatic. Claude has an API behind it — Claude Teams is the human-facing wrapper.
A long secret string that authorizes software to call an API on your behalf. Like a password but for code. Stored carefully — never pasted into a chat, never put in a public spreadsheet.

When Claude decides to use a connected tool to get information (e.g., look up a Shopify order) rather than guessing. You'll see this as "Claude is searching Shopify…" mid-conversation. It's how Claude stays accurate.

The math behind the Vault. Documents get turned into a kind of meaning-fingerprint, and queries find the closest-meaning ones — even if the words don't match. It's why "how do we ship to a wholesale account" finds the right SOP even if the SOP says "B2B fulfillment."
The "Sign in with Google" button, basically. Lets one app trust your login from another (Google) without ever seeing your password. That's how Claude Teams knows you're you when you click sign-in.

Three names for the same thing: the boundary around "Pappy & Co's stuff" inside a vendor's app. Our Claude Teams workspace is the Pappy bubble — what's in it stays in it, separate from any other company's workspace.
All three mean the same thing: one back-and-forth with Claude. Each is independent (Claude forgets the last one when you start a new one — unless it's in the same project's saved conversations).

A repeatable way we do something. "Drafting a wholesale follow-up" is a workflow; "replying to a Gorgias ticket" is a workflow. Each workflow has its own level of AI oversight that the team agrees on.

Software running a workflow without a person clicking each step. The opposite of "manually". When we say a workflow is "automated," we mean AI runs it within agreed rules; a person reviews on a defined cadence.
Sandbox = a safe play area for testing (no real customers see the output). Production = the real thing, customer-facing. We try things in sandbox first.

Personally Identifiable Information — anything that could identify a real person (name + email, full credit card, home address, etc.). Pappy's Tier 1 list includes a lot of PII; that's why it never goes near Claude.
A record of who did what, when. Claude Teams keeps one (every conversation, every connector use). It's how we can investigate "did this go wrong?" without trusting memory.

LLM = Large Language Model (Claude, GPT, Gemini — the big general-purpose ones). SLM = Small Language Model — smaller, faster, runs on a phone or a small server for specific tasks. The press talks about both.
ML = Machine Learning (the broader field; LLMs are one part of it). NLP = Natural Language Processing (working with text specifically). LLMs are NLP done at huge scale.

Artificial General Intelligence — a hypothetical AI as broadly capable as a human across every domain. We don't have it. When you see "AGI" in the news, it's usually speculative. What we have today (LLMs like Claude) is narrower — very good at text, not capable of reasoning about the physical world the way a person is.

areasSection.title: THREE THINGS THAT MATTER.
areasSection.deck: That's it. No plan to track, nothing to fill in.

areas.title: USE THE TOOL YOU'LL ACTUALLY USE.
areas.deck: Every major model is excellent now. The one that makes you productive is the one you're comfortable in — so pick that one, and the company will pay for it.

points.title: If you like ChatGPT, use ChatGPT.
points.bodyHtml: Have fun with it. If you're comfortable in that UX, you've built up context and information in there, and you're using it daily — keep doing exactly that. I'm happy to set up ChatGPT on your desktop, which includes Codex alongside it. It functions essentially the same as Claude, and it does the same data connectors: Shopify, Google Workspace, Meta Ads, Klaviyo.

points.title: Gemini and Grok count too.
points.bodyHtml: Same deal. We keep the same amount of AI either way — one seat per person, whichever platform that seat is on. It's basically the same cost per month, so if you'd feel more comfortable somewhere else, we're happy to switch your seat from one platform to the other. Just ask.

points.title: For super users: switch whenever you like.
points.bodyHtml: At least between OpenAI and Anthropic, all the models are extremely good and extremely powerful right now. It genuinely doesn't matter which one you're on — what matters is that you're comfortable enough in it to try ambitious things.

points.title: Where I've landed, for what it's worth.
points.bodyHtml: I'm using ChatGPT about 85% of the time now and Claude about 15% — and that 15% is a few hyper-specific things I'm doing. OpenAI is also more efficient and cheaper at the moment. That may well not be true in three months; these things change by the month. Don't overthink it, and don't feel you have to follow me.

points.title: The company covers it.
points.bodyHtml: Pick the platform you're comfortable doing cool stuff in, and Pappy & Company will cover the subscription for the leadership team. The small monthly fee is not the thing worth optimizing — your comfort with the tool is.

areas.noteHtml: Two things stay the same whichever platform you pick. Use the seat the company provides rather than a personal free account, and the data tiers in the docs below apply identically everywhere. Those rules were never really about Claude — they're about where Pappy's information is allowed to go.

areas.title: THE KNOWLEDGE BASE IS THE ASSET.
areas.deck: The models will keep changing, month to month. What compounds is what we know. It's the most important thing we have as a company, and maintaining it is the most important thing we can do.

points.title: What it is — and what it isn't.
points.bodyHtml: This has nothing to do with the data already sitting in our platforms. Shopify, Cin7, Klaviyo, Attentive, GA4 — those are connected, and any of the tools can query them directly. The knowledge base is ours: our internal processes and structures, tribal knowledge, the things we've learned the hard way, financial contracts, vendor contracts. Today it's scattered across the Google Shared Drive, buried in email threads, and held in people's heads.

points.title: The hard part is maintenance, not collection.
points.bodyHtml: Getting documents in is easy. Keeping them trustworthy is the actual work — stale data, overlapping data, duplicates, and documents that flatly contradict each other. One confidently wrong answer costs more trust than ten right ones earn, so the controls matter more than the volume.

points.title: Getting something in should take five seconds.
points.bodyHtml: In Google Chat, @ the assistant and say “add this document.” That's the whole process. No form, no folder to remember, no meeting. Zero friction is the point — the moment it takes effort, it stops happening.

points.title: Everyone submits. Leadership approves.
points.bodyHtml: Anyone on the leadership team and frontline managers — Candice, Kaitlyn, whoever is closest to the actual work — can submit. At the end of the week, one or two people on leadership approve or decline the new additions, and the approved ones get fed in.

points.title: Structure on the way in is what makes it work.
points.bodyHtml: Every document gets parsed into clean metadata: what it is, which vendor it relates to, what it covers, how current it is — organized consistently so any AI tool or agent can reference and pull the right thing quickly and accurately. It's invisible when it's done right and worthless when it isn't.

points.title: This is the part that's actually ours.
points.bodyHtml: Platforms change. The knowledge base doesn't — it moves with us to whatever tool we're on next. Of everything on this page, it's the one piece that compounds.

areas.title: DO IT IN THE OPEN.
areas.deck: There is real skill, nuance and artistry in this — especially as we move from simple chat to agentic tasks. Nobody learns that siloed.

points.title: A channel for it, open to everyone.
points.bodyHtml: A separate Google Chat channel where anyone at Pappy & Company can share the cool thing they did with AI, how they did it, how something broke, what they learned from it, and the tips, tricks and skills they've picked up.

points.title: Post the failures too. Especially those.
points.bodyHtml: Watching somebody work through a strange edge case teaches far more than a polished result does. There's real communication and perseverance involved in getting these things to work — that part is invisible unless we show it.

points.title: You can't learn this alone.
points.bodyHtml: It's extremely hard for anyone non-technical to get good at this in isolation. YouTube covers the generic case; it will never cover a Pappy wholesale bundle, a Cerity report, or how our vendor history is organized. That nuance only exists here, and it only spreads if we show it to each other.

points.title: Non-judgmental, on purpose.
points.bodyHtml: Celebrating successes and failures both, watching each other work, nobody made to feel behind. That is the only way all of us get more skilled at this.

points.title: It's where the industry has gone.
points.bodyHtml: Whether it's Slack or Microsoft Teams, this is how it's being used at Shopify, at Anthropic, and at the digital ad agencies. AI lives in the communication channels now — out in the open, collaboratively shared, referenced and pulled together. An open transaction log everyone can watch and learn from.

areas.noteHtml: This is the next phase of bringing AI into our Google Chat space. Culture and skill spread bottom-up and organically — not from a training deck.
